slides.title: Introduction to Computer Vision
slides.text:
Introduction to Computer Vision

•  Computer vision: A multidisciplinary field that seeks to describe the three-
   dimensional world through two-dimensional imagery and mimic the
   sophisticated visual perception of biological systems.
•  The most fundamental way to define computer vision is as the inverse problem
   of computer graphics.
•  While computer graphics generates realistic 2D images from 3D digital models
   (3D), computer vision attempts to take one or more 2D images & reconstruct
   the properties of the 3D world that produced them.
•  The goal is to describe and reconstruct properties such as:
    – Shape: The geometric structure of objects.
    –  Illumination: The sources and intensity of light.
    –  Color Distributions: How light interacts with surfaces

                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: Vision described as inverse of graphics: 2D observations infer 3D world properties, whereas graphics renders 3D models. Desired properties shape, illumination and color distributions. Inverse does not imply unique reconstruction.

slides.title: Introduction to Computer Vision (Cont.)
slides.text:
Introduction to Computer Vision (Cont.)
•  Inherent Challenges and Ambiguities
    –  In computer vision, the process of image formation involves a projection of the 3D
       world onto a 2D surface, resulting in the loss of depth information.
    –  This creates a mathematical ambiguity: an image cannot inherently distinguish
      between a large object afar and identical-looking object closer to the sensor.
•  Human Vision Vs Computer vision





                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Projection loses depth; apparent size alone cannot distinguish size/distance. Figure contrasts human object labels Chair/Dog/Tree/Table with robot Feature extraction/Edge detection/Uncertainty and Object?; schematic is not a theorem that machines cannot recognize objects.

slides.text:
Evolution and History

 The history of computer vision is a progression from early attempts at basic scene
 understanding to the mathematically rigorous and data-driven approaches of the
 modern era.





                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Diagram adds extracted-text-missing history: 1970s early scene understanding includes line labeling (3D from 2D line drawings), pictorial structures (flexible parts), Marr’s Paradigm with Computational Theory (Goal), Algorithm (Method), then a repeated Marr’s Paradigm bullet instead of a distinct third level. 1980s: pyramids/scale-space multi-resolution, regularization smoothness for ill-posed problems, MRF probabilistic global optimization. 1990s–Present: SfM reconstruction, computational photography HDR/panoramas/texture synthesis, deep learning. slides.title: Real-World Applications
slides.text:
Real-World Applications

•   Industrial Applications
   Computer vision is deeply integrated into industrial workflows:
    –  Optical Character Recognition (OCR): Reading text from documents or packages.
    –  Mechanical Inspection: Automatically checking manufacturing tolerances or finding defects.
    –  Medical Imaging: Analyzing CT or MRI scans for diagnosis.
    –  Autonomous Systems: Enabling self-driving cars and drones to navigate using SLAM.
•  Consumer Applications
   Vision technology is ubiquitous in consumer electronics:
    –  Image Stitching: Creating panoramas on smartphones.
    –  Augmented Reality (AR): Inserting 3D virtual models into live video
        feeds by tracking reference points.
    –  Biometrics: Using face and fingerprint recognition for device
         authentication.
    –  Visual Effects: Morphing images and stabilizing shaky video.

                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Eight named mappings: OCR documents/packages; mechanical inspection tolerances/defects; medical CT/MRI analysis; autonomous vehicles/drones and SLAM; image stitching panoramas; AR tracked reference points with virtual models in live feed; biometrics face/fingerprint authentication; visual effects morphing/stabilization.

slides.title: Fundamentals of Vision - Light
slides.text:
Fundamentals of Vision - Light

•   Light is a form of electromagnetic radiation with a
   mixture of many wavelengths, represented as a function
   E(λ) describing intensity as a function of wavelength.
•  As light travels through a medium (like air or water), its
   spectrum is modified by absorption and thus transmits
   modified spectrum.                                              Blackbody emissions for
•   In 1670, Sir Isaac Newton discovered (through refraction)      the Sun (5778 K),
                                                                     a tungsten lamp (2600 K)
   that white light is a mixture of different colors, each
   corresponding to a specific wavelength.
•  The human eye perceives wavelengths
   between approximately 400 nm and
   700 nm as distinct colors.


                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: E(lambda) spectral intensity; medium absorption changes spectrum; slide attributes white-light dispersion to Newton in1670. Approximate visible range400–700nm. Plot normalized intensity versus wavelength300–1000nm: orange Sun5778K peaks around500nm; blue Lamp2600K rises across plotted interval, reaching its displayed maximum at1000nm. Independent normalization means no absolute emitted-power inference. Rainbow400–750nm. Do not infer lamp true peak is1000nm from plot boundary.

slides.title: Machine Vision - Image Signal Processor (ISP)
slides.text:
Machine Vision - Image Signal Processor (ISP)

•  Demosaicing:
    –  Since each pixel only measures one color (R, G, or B), the ISP of the camera must
       estimate the other two-color values via interpolation from neighboring pixels.
    – Thus converting "mosaic" single-color pixels into 3 complete R, G, and B color planes
•  Denoising:
    – Sensor data is subject to various types of noise, such as shot noise (photon count
        variance) and dark current (thermal electrons).
    – The ISP applies filters to reduce this graininess, especially in
        low-light regions.
•  Sharpening:
    – Edge-enhancement filters are applied to compensate for the
        blur introduced by the lens and the demosaicing process.


                                                                                                          17

visualInspection.notes: Demosaicing estimates two missing color values per CFA pixel via neighbors, producing three color planes. Shot noise identified as photon-count variance, dark current as thermal electrons. Denoising reduces graininess especially low light. Sharpening edge enhancement compensates lens/demosaic blur; cannot assume perfect detail recovery.

slides.title: Machine Vision - Image Signal Processor (ISP) (Cont.)
slides.text:
Machine Vision - Image Signal Processor (ISP) (Cont.)

•  White Balancing
    –  Ensures that a white object appears white (equal RGB values) under different light
       sources (e.g., yellow tungsten vs. blue sky), the ISP applies gains to the channels.
•  Color Correction
    –  Since the spectral sensitivities of camera filters do not perfectly match human cone
       responses, the ISP uses a 3×3 or 3×4 camera matrix (C) to "twist" the color space into
       a standardized format like CIE XYZ (device-independent color space) or sRGB.
•  Gamma Encoding/Compression
    – Human vision is roughly logarithmic, so ISPs use power-law
      (gamma) correction to match perception and display
       response.
•   Final Compression to JPEG image.


                                                                                                          18

visualInspection.notes: White balance channel gains aim for neutral equal RGB under illuminant changes. Color correction uses3x3 or3x4 C mapping camera responses toward CIE XYZ/sRGB because camera filters do not perfectly match cones. This color matrix C is not the later geometric3x4 camera projection matrix C. Gamma power-law encoding approximates perceptual/display response and is distinct from final JPEG compression; no exact gamma exponent or universal log law specified.

slides.title: Geometric Image Formation - Image models
slides.text:
Geometric Image Formation – Image models
•  Image formation is the physical process
    in which light reflected from a surface is
   collected and focused by a camera’s
    optical system.
•   It fundamentally projects data from the
   three-dimensional world into two-
   dimensional image plane.
                                                               Simplified model of image formation [1]
•  The depth information is lost, and we
   can no longer tell from the image
   whether it is of a large object in the
   distance, or a smaller, closer object.





                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Actual diagram: light source illuminates a surface with normal n-hat; scattered rays include green ray through optics O to rear sensor plane. A separate virtual image plane is in front. Image formation maps 3D to 2D with depth loss; do not confuse physical rear sensor with front virtual plane.

slides.title: Geometric Image Formation - Pinhole
slides.text:
Geometric Image Formation – Image models

• Models of Projection - Pinhole & Lens-based
•  Pinhole Camera model:
   – Simplest form of image formation
   – Light from the scene passes through a small
       aperture, casting an inverted image on the opposite
                                                                 Pin Hole Camera Model [2]        wall.
   – No focus needed, generates dim image.





                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Upright object left, small aperture middle, inverted smaller real image right. Ideal pinhole requires no focusing adjustment but transmits little light. Do not extend ideal ray model to unlimited sharpness or ignore diffraction when making physical claims.

   imaging model.

   image.

   transformation, we represent both 3D world points, and

slides.title: Perspective Projection (Cont.)
slides.text:
Central Perspective Imaging Model - Discrete Image Plane
                                                   •   In a digital camera, the image plane
                                                              is comprised of a W×H grid of light-
                                                 sensitive elements called photosites
                                             (with side lengths w and h).
                                                   •  By convention, the origin (0,0) is

slides.title: Projection of Group of Points/Primitives
slides.text:
Projection of Group of Points/Primitives

•  A critical feature of digital sensing is visibility checking, which determines
   whether a projected 3D point actually falls within the physical boundaries of
   the sensor (W×H pixels).
•  Projecting a regular grid of points is a common way to visualize the geometric
   effects of perspective projection.
    –  In a frontal view, the grid appears regular and symmetric.
    –  In an oblique view (captured by changing the camera pose), the grid shape is
        distorted.
    –  Parallel edges in the world are projected as lines that
       converge toward a vanishing point.
•  Beyond simple points, the toolbox can project complex
  3D primitives like cubes.


                                                                                                          28

visualInspection.notes: Visibility tests sensor W×H boundaries; regular frontal grid versus distorted oblique view; says parallel world edges converge to a vanishing point without qualifying directions parallel to image plane. Add positive camera-depth condition for physical visibility and note no occlusion model. Cubes introduced as projectable primitives.

    –  Shifting of cube in opposite direction

       converges to a vanishing point.

visualInspection.notes: Exact wireframe code X,Y,Z=mkcube(0.2,pose=SE3.Tz(1),edge=True); camera.plot_wireframe(X,Y,Z); T_camera=SE3.Trans(-0.25,0,0); camera.plot_wireframe(X,Y,Z,pose=T_camera). Imports of mkcube/SE3 and camera setup not repeated. Figures show two depth faces and changed side-edge slopes after camera moves left. Text claim coplanar edges/lines remain parallel is overbroad/false: depth-directed parallel lines are also coplanar; directions parallel to image plane preserve parallelism, directions with nonzero depth component have finite vanishing point (nondegenerate projection). Near/far faces shift by different amounts under translation.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  Computer vision reconstructs 3D world properties (shape, illumination, color)
   from 2D images.
•   It mimics biological eye (camera) and brain (algorithms) to enable intelligence.
•  Projecting the 3D world onto a 2D surface causes loss of depth information,
   creating mathematical ambiguity between object size and distance.
•   Digital sensing pipeline involves optics for image capturing, while electronics for
   sensing and signal processing to generate image.
•  Pinhole or lens-based models are used to focus and
   project light onto an image plane.
•  Camera Matrix (C) maps 3D points to 2D pixels by
   combining intrinsic (internal camera geometry) and
    extrinsic (camera pose) parameters.

                                                                                                          31
slides.exclusionReason: Recapitulates924–950; substantive earlier concepts retain links, no duplicate question count.

visualInspection.notes: Six recap bullets repeat inverse vision, eye/brain, depth loss, optics/electronics, pinhole/lens and camera intrinsic/extrinsic matrix. Pinhole/lens grouped as focus and project, but pinhole geometrically selects rays, not refractive focusing. No new unique formula or procedure beyond earlier pages.
